sos.s: A toddler melting down on the floor
sos.me: Your child's emotions are like waves, not an attempt to defeat you; you are their lighthouse. Slow your own breathing first, and your voice will slow too.
go: Get down to your child's eye level and lower your voice
Name the feeling: “You're really angry / disappointed.” Receive the emotion before giving reasons
Keep everyone safe: move dangerous things away; hold them or stay close and wait
sos.say: “I know you're really upset. I'm right here with you. When you're ready, we'll work it out together.”
sos.after: Once calm, hug them and state the boundary in a sentence or two (“Being angry is okay; hitting is not”), then pray: “Jesus, thank you for loving us even when we're angry.”

sos.me: A child's “no” is often practice at growing up, not a challenge to your authority. Don't turn it into a battle someone has to win.
go: Turn commands into limited choices: “Teeth first or pajamas first?”
Say it once — clear, gentle, firm — then give them a little time
Calmly carry out the consequence you agreed beforehand; don't add more or bring up the past
sos.say: “I love you, so this still needs doing. You can choose how to do it.”
sos.after: Afterward, affirm what they did manage and ask what was going on inside. Check yourself: were my instructions too many or too fast?

sos.me: You are not the judge but the peacemaker. Don't rush to decide who's right; first make everyone safe and quiet.
go: Separate first: “Let's pause. Everyone sit in a different spot.”
Take turns: each says “I feel… because…”; others only listen
Let them come up with a solution; you just help check it's fair
sos.say: “In our family it's okay to be angry, but not to hurt each other. Let's work out how to make peace.”
sos.after: After making up, say “I'm sorry, please forgive me” to each other, then hug or high-five. At bedtime, each says one thing they're thankful for in the other.

sos.me: Being a few minutes late costs less than a wounded heart. Today's rush shouldn't become a whole day's hurt.
go: Give only the next step: “Shoes on now.” One instruction at a time
Use a timer or a song instead of nagging
If you really will be late, let the natural consequence happen (explain to the teacher) rather than lecturing on the way
sos.say: “We can do this together. I'll get your bag; you're in charge of your shoes.”
sos.after: In a calm moment tonight, decide together what to prepare earlier tomorrow, and draw a “morning routine” chart for the door.

sos.s: The whole family is falling apart
sos.me: Neither your worth nor your child's rests on this worksheet. Relationship matters more than marks; people matter more than tasks.
go: Stop for five minutes: drink water, move, breathe
Break the big task into small steps, one at a time
Stay close but don't do it for them; when stuck ask, “What do you think the first step is?”
sos.say: “It's okay that this one is hard. We'll go step by step. I care about you, not just your marks.”
sos.after: At bedtime, praise effort rather than results. If it happens often, talk with the teacher about the workload or learning approach.

sos.me: Your child isn't bad; they're hooked by something designed to be hard to put down. Check your family agreement — and your own phone.
go: Give warning: “Ten more minutes, then it's off.” Remind them again when time's up
Let them press “off” themselves, giving a sense of control
Follow straight away with something real: a snack together, a walk outside
sos.say: “I know it's fun and hard to stop. Let's keep our agreement; there's time again tomorrow.”
sos.after: At a calm time, revise your screen agreement as a family (add it to “Our family agreements”). Parents keep it too.

sos.me: Children often lie because they're afraid. If telling the truth costs too much, they learn to hide. Make home a place where truth is safe.
go: Don't interrogate; give a chance to be honest: “I want to hear what really happened.”
When they tell the truth, first affirm their courage, then deal with the issue
Aim consequences at the behavior; don't label them a “liar”
sos.say: “Thank you for telling me the truth. That wasn't easy. Let's face this together.”
sos.after: Share a time you were afraid to tell the truth, read “putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor” together, and pray for honest hearts.

sos.s: One sentence sets you on fire
sos.me: Pride provokes pride and both lose; humility draws out humility and both win. You don't need to win this sentence.
go: Don't snap back; breathe and halve your volume
Calmly name the tone: “I want to hear your view, but please say it respectfully.”
If you're both too heated, agree to talk again in ten minutes
sos.say: “I want to understand what you mean. Could you say it again more calmly?”
sos.after: Afterward, apologize first for your part (if any), then listen for what they really meant. Backchat often hides a need that's been overlooked.

sos.me: A closed door isn't always rejection; often they haven't found the words yet. Relationship matters more than being right, and waiting is also love.
go: Don't press; leave a note or message: “I'm here whenever you want to talk.”
Make side-by-side time: driving, walking, a late snack — easier than face-to-face
When they do open up, listen to the end before advising or commenting
sos.say: “You don't have to talk now. I just want you to know that whatever happens, I love you and I'm on your side.”
sos.after: Pray for them, and ask yourself: have I been talking more than listening lately? If you see signs of self-harm, bullying or depression, seek a counselor and your pastor.

sos.me: You are not a failed parent; you are a person who needs God to hold you up. Looking after yourself is not selfish — it's so you can keep loving.
go: If it's safe, step away for a minute or two and tell your child: “I need to calm down. I'll be right back.”
Drink a glass of water, breathe slowly ten times, and tell the Lord: “I can't do this — help me.”
Lower the bar today: a simple dinner, chores tomorrow; call your spouse or a spiritual companion
sos.say: “I'm really tired right now and need a short break. It's not your fault. I'll be back soon.”
sos.after: Plan some real rest for yourself tonight. If you're struggling with ongoing sleeplessness, low mood or anger you can't control, please see a doctor, a counselor and your pastor.

steps.d: Admit your wrong, receive the Lord's forgiveness, and let your heart settle.
Don't apologize while emotions are still high; kneel down and look your child in the eye.
“I shouted at you just now and said hurtful things.” Not “But you also…”.

steps.t: Acknowledge the effect on your child
steps.d: “You must have felt scared and sad.”

steps.t: Say how you'll change and ask forgiveness
steps.d: “Next time I'm angry I'll stop and breathe first. Will you forgive me?”
Don't demand instant forgiveness, and don't trade your apology for theirs.

say: “I'm sorry I shouted at you. That was my fault, not yours.”
“The way I spoke hurt you. I love you, and I'm learning gentleness from Jesus.”
“Will you forgive me? Shall we pray to Jesus together?”
